sentences.text: The generic name Peloroplites combines Greek words meaning "monstrous" and "heavily armed soldier," while the specific name cedrimontanus refers to the Cedar Mountain Formation in Latin.

Scientists diagnose this animal by features such as the lack of premaxillary teeth, a sloping occiput, absence of a prominent lateral temporal notch, small squamosal horns, and specific skull proportions.
The snout of Peloroplites tapers to a relatively broad premaxillary beak, which contrasts with the narrower beak found in the genus Silvisaurus.
The jugal-quadratojugal horncores of Peloroplites appear as low, localized bone thickenings and are not prominent like those seen in Gastonia and Animantarx.
The centra of Peloroplites have a strongly concave ventral margin and steeply angled prezygapophyses.
The synsacrum of Peloroplites is made of six fused vertebrae, a condition shared with the genus Silvisaurus.
Metacarpal I is the largest metacarpal in the hand and lacks distal condyles.
The skull lacked premaxillary teeth and possessed a beak, with only modest horn-like projections, while the jaws, represented by their posterior halves, were constructed heavily.
The preacetabular process of the pelvis diverges at 55 degrees, which differs from the divergence seen in Sauropelta and Edmontonia.
The ilia appear unusually oriented outward with an inclination of 55 degrees compared to the approximately 30 or 40 degrees of other nodosaurids, though this might be a preservation effect.
Carpenter et al. originally estimated Peloroplites to be 5 to 5.5 meters long, while Gregory S. Paul later estimated it to be 6 meters long and weigh 2 tonnes.
The large adductor fossa and large teeth suggest Peloroplites may have eaten tougher forage, a diet supported by evidence of robust jaws.
The genus Peloroplites was named in 2008 by Kenneth Carpenter and colleagues, with the genus authority and species authority for P. cedrimontanus both attributed to Carpenter et al., 2008.

A skeleton of a large nodosaurid from the Price River II quarry in Emery County, Utah, was first mentioned in 2001 by Burge and Bird, and additional material was described in 2008 by Kenneth Carpenter, Jeff Bartlett, John Bird, and Reese Barrick.
Peloroplites is known from a postcranial skeleton and a skull found in the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in Emery County, Utah.
The holotype and assigned specimens are housed at the College of Eastern Utah Prehistoric Museum in Utah.
Diet: Large teeth and robust jaws suggest Peloroplites consumed tougher forage than other ankylosaurians.
Growth: The total number of vertebrae in Peloroplites is unknown because the atlas vertebra has not been discovered.
Carpenter et al. (2008) originally classified Peloroplites within the family Nodosauridae without performing a detailed phylogenetic analysis.
Thompson et al. (2012) and Chen et al. (2013) both recovered Peloroplites as the sister taxon to Polacanthus.

Yang et al. (2013) placed Peloroplites as sister to both Taohelong and Polacanthus, whereas Zheng et al. (2018) found it sister to Taohelong and a large clade including Nodosaurus, Edmontonia, Struthiosaurus, and Europelta.
Rivera-Sylva et al. (2018) placed Peloroplites as the sister taxon to Sauropelta, Taohelong, and a clade of more nested taxa.
The layer containing Peloroplites was originally interpreted as Aptian to Albian age, approximately 109 to 116 million years ago.
Other radiometric dates place the Mussentuchit Member in the Cenomanian to early Turonian age, between 98.2 ± 0.6 and 93 million years ago.
The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Peloroplites as Aptian to Albian, from 121.4 to 100.5 million years ago.
Researchers suggested that some nodosaurid material previously identified as Sauropelta might actually belong to Peloroplites.
One specimen tentatively referred to Sauropelta could not be assigned to either that genus or Peloroplites.
There is an ongoing debate regarding the exact phylogenetic position of Peloroplites, with different studies placing it in varying relationships to genera like Polacanthus, Taohelong, and Nodosaurus.
